SECTION: Chapter 1: Historical Overview of Hamilton County (Pages 9-20)

TOPICS: Early exploration and settlement, Native American history, land surveying, railroad development, agricultural history, town development, county seat disputes, population trends, ethnic settlements, religious institutions

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Early explorers like Lewis and Clark and Zebulon Pike described Nebraska as unproductive, leading to the term "Great American Desert" (Page 9)
- General Stephen Kearney led an expedition through Hamilton County in 1835, and J. P. Elliot later settled there (Page 9)
- General John C. Fremont crossed the county in 1842, a route later followed by the Mormons (Page 9)
- Native American groups included the Pawnees, Iowas, Omahas, Otos, Missourias, and Poncas (Page 9)
- The territory including part of present-day Hamilton County was ceded to the government by Native Americans in 1833 (Page 9)
- The Nebraska Territory was organized in 1854, and Nebraska became the 37th state in 1867 (Page 9)
- The United States Public Land Survey (Land Ordinance of 1785) established the township and range system (Page 9)
- Two congressional acts in 1862 (Transcontinental Railroad Act and Homestead Act) profoundly impacted Nebraska (Page 10)
- The Union Pacific Railroad traversed 472 miles from Omaha to the Colorado border and was completed in less than three years (Page 10)
- The Homestead Act provided pioneers 160 acres of land if they built a permanent structure and lived on it for five years (Page 10)
- By 1900, almost 69,000 people had acquired land in Nebraska under the Homestead Act (Page 10)
- Nearly half (43 percent) of those who filed Homestead claims in Nebraska failed to secure title to the land (Page 10)
- The earliest settlement in Hamilton County began in 1861 with the creation of the Nebraska City-Fort Kearny cut-off (Page 10)
- David Millspaw established a ranch in 1861 in Section 11, Township 10, Range 5 (Page 10)
- John Harris and Alfred Blue set up the "Deep Well Ranch" in 1862 (Page 10)
- Hamilton County's boundaries were officially established in 1867 at statehood (Page 10)
- The county was named for Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury (Page 10)
- The county was not organized until 1870 following a general election held at John Harris' house (Page 10)
- The first county seat was Orville City, named for Orville Westcott (Page 10)
- In 1879, the first railroad line reached Hamilton County from York to Aurora (Page 10)
- 66-1/3 miles of railroad lines were in operation in Hamilton County (Page 11)
- By 1927, Hamilton County had direct railroad connections from Aurora to Omaha, Lincoln, and other important cities of Nebraska (Page 11)
- Several major automobile routes serve Hamilton County: State Highway 14, US Highway 34, and Interstate 80 (Page 11)
- Construction of Interstate 80 in Nebraska began in 1957 near Gretna and was completed in 1974 near Sidney for a total length of 455 miles (Page 11)
- Hamilton County is located in the southeastern part of Nebraska in the Central Loess Plains (Page 11)
- Hamilton County covers approximately 538 square miles (Page 11)
- Elevations range from 1,660 feet above sea level in the east to nearly 1,900 feet in the west (Page 11)
- The Platte River valley dominates the county's northern boundary and is approximately 100 feet below the county's general level (Page 11)
- Hamilton County's first permanent settlement took place in June of 1866 (Page 11)
- Jarvil Chaffee established a homestead in Section 34, Township 9, Range 6 (HM00-122) in 1872 (Page 12)
- Chaffee's Homestead Certificate was signed by Ulysses S. Grant on May 1, 1872 (Page 12)
- James Waddle and John Brown settled in Section 26, Township 9, Range 5 in January 1867 (Page 12)
- Hamilton County's population grew from 130 in 1870 to 8,267 in 1880 and reached its peak of 14,096 in 1890 (Page 12)
- By 1885, there were ninety-eight organized rural school districts in the county (Page 12)
- Most early settlers came from Missouri, Iowa, Illinois, Ohio, and the New England States; later immigrants came from Germany, Sweden, England, and Russia (Page 12)
- Ethnic groups settled in clusters: Danes in the northeast, Swedes in the northwest, Irish, Bohemians, and Germans in the southwest, and Russian Mennonites in the southeast (Page 12)
- The Danish culture of the Kronborg area is described as flourishing (Page 13)
- The Swedish culture of Hordville and environs is mentioned (Page 13)
- The Russian German culture extends west into Hamilton County from the Henderson [York County] region (Page 13)
- The Irish settled west of Aurora in towns like Murphy (Page 13)
- A Danish Lutheran Church (HM05-001) had some 200 families (Page 13)
- The "Danes of Kronborg" have retained the closest ties to their Scandinavian heritage (Page 13)
- Lives of Danish immigrants around Kronborg centered on the congregation at St. John’s (Page 13)
- St. John’s complex continues to dominate the area and serve as a focal point for the community (Page 13)
- Zion Lutheran Church and School (HM00-045) is located in northeastern Hamilton County (Page 13)
- The area was settled by Germans and the first church was erected in 1877 (Page 13)
- The present Zion Lutheran Church was dedicated in 1897 (Page 13)
- The exterior of the church was altered in 1972 when a new foyer was added (Page 13)
- A large U-shaped balcony wraps around three sides of the nave at Zion Lutheran Church (Page 13)
- Pressed tin is found throughout the building at Zion Lutheran Church (Page 13)
- Farming has always been the major occupation in Hamilton County (Page 14)
- Corn was the dominant crop even before widespread irrigation (Page 14)
- In 1890, Hamilton County had 119,237 acres in corn and 48,960 acres in wheat (Page 14)
- In 1900, there were over 2,000 individual farms; by the mid-1960s, there were nearly 1,100 (Page 14)
- In 1920, the average farm size was 179.7 acres (Page 14)
- In 1997, there were 697 farms averaging 507 acres (Page 14)
- By 2002, there were 603 farms averaging 577 acres (Page 14)
- In 2002, Hamilton County ranked first in Nebraska in the value of crops produced (Page 14)
- Hamilton County annually receives approximately twenty-six inches of precipitation (Page 14)
- Irrigation canals and wells first appeared in Hamilton County in the late 1930s (Page 15)
- In August 1940, The Aurora News published a photo comparing a successful irrigated corn crop (80 bushels) to a failed dryland crop (Page 15)
- By February 1955, the 500th well was drilled, and the county was declared "The Deepwell Irrigation Center of the Nation" (Page 15)
- By the late 1960s, there were approximately 1,600 registered wells irrigating over 100,000 acres (Page 15)
- In the early 1970s, center-pivot irrigation systems reached the county, leading to a rapid conversion of rangeland to cropland (Page 15)
- By the late 1970s, about 89% of the county's area was cropland, with 81% irrigated and 19% dryfarmed (Page 15)
- In the early 1980s, the number of irrigation wells had increased to over 2,600 (Page 15)
- As of the time of writing, Hamilton County has 3,361 irrigation wells that water just over 400,000 acres (Page 15)
- The first farmers' elevator in Hordville incorporated in 1906, and by 1915 all communities had elevators (Page 15)
- In 1921, Burr and Buck claimed Hamilton is the only county in Nebraska, or probably any other state, with a farmers' elevator at every railroad station (Page 16)
- Grain elevators in Hamilton County's communities are the largest structures and serve as one of each town's focal points (Page 16)
- Many of the county's original towns are no longer present due to population shifts related to changing economic issues and transportation patterns (Page 16)
- Baltensperger contends that town development became heavily dependent on rail connections (Page 16)
- The town of Hamilton, founded by J. F. and T. H. Glover, was an active place in 1874-75 but lost its businesses and houses when the county seat was located in Aurora (Page 16)
- Most early settlements like Alvin, Avon, Buckeye, Bunker Hill, Cedar Valley, Leonard, Lerton, Mirimichi, Orville City, Otis, Penn, Shiloh, Stockham, St. Joe, and Williamsport have disappeared (Page 17)
- Of the remaining towns, Giltner, Hampton, Marquette, Murphy, and Phillips are located on the railroad (Page 17)
- Towns were platted as square blocks and designed as T-Towns, with Main Street beginning at the railroad tracks (Page 17)
- Five of the seven rural communities peaked in population between 1900 and 1940 (Page 17)
- Four of those five communities have demonstrated recent population gains (Page 17)
- Aurora peaked in population at the most recent census in 2000 with 4,225 citizens and has steadily increased since 1940 (Page 17)
- Farm consolidation is expected to make it difficult for towns outside of Aurora to maintain their populations (Page 17)
- Pat Dinslage (1992) discusses population declines in Hordville (pop. 150) and Polk (pop. 322), noting their dependence on farming communities (Page 18)
- Bradley Baltensperger (1985) describes county seat disputes in frontier Nebraska as involving fraudulent elections, theft of records, and court battles (Page 18)
- Orville City was selected as the first county seat in 1871 but was challenged for being too far southeast (Page 18)
- In the first election, Aurora received over two-thirds of the votes but the results were deemed illegal (Page 18)
- A second vote in 1874 required 399.5 votes; Aurora collected 399, failing by half a vote (Page 18)
- Aurora citizens took possession of the county courthouse and records by force in 1874 (Page 18)
- Darius Wilcox lobbied the state legislature to change the requirement to three-fifths of votes cast (Page 18)
- A special election in May saw Aurora win by a small majority, while Hamilton won the June election by a slim margin (Page 18)
- The fifth and final vote in October 1875 resulted in Aurora receiving 481 votes and Hamilton 400, making Aurora the official seat of government in early 1876 (Page 18)
- After the election, Hamilton and Orville merged with Aurora, and Hamilton became a "deserted village" (Page 18)
- In 1871, David Stone represented a group of men from Lucas County, Iowa, who wished to establish a town in Hamilton County (Page 18)
- The town of Aurora was founded in 1871 at a point on Lincoln Creek where two cottonwood trees stood (Page 19)
- The site is now part of Streeter Park (HM01-243) (Page 19)
- David Stone erected the "first frame building in the town" in August 1871, a store and residence (Page 19)
- The town was named for Stone's hometown, Aurora, Illinois (Page 19)
- Aurora was incorporated on July 3, 1877 (Page 19)
- The Burlington and Missouri Railroad arrived in 1879, which was a major turning point (Page 19)
- The railroad required a $72,000 bond, with $48,000 due when the line reached Aurora (Page 19)
- A vote on the bond resulted in 956 votes in favor and 238 opposed out of 1,194 cast (Page 19)
- The bond amount was lowered to $50,000 due to public support (Page 19)
- The first regular train ran into Aurora on October 14, 1879 (Page 19)
- The railroad extended lines from Aurora west to Grand Island (1884) and north to Central City (1886) (Page 19)
- Aurora was Hamilton County's primary city in the late 1800s and early 1900s (Page 20)
- Early enterprises included a cigar factory, a broom factory, and a washing machine company (Page 20)
- The Temple Craft Association was formed in 1888 by thirty-one men to promote Aurora's business community (Page 20)
- Fourteen leading business men pledged $25,000 in capital for the Temple Craft project (Page 20)
- The Hamilton County Bank was established in 1877 by George Wildish (Page 20)
- The Farmers' and Merchants' Bank was established in 1883 by Streeter, Hainer, and Farley (Page 20)
- Several banks merged to form the First National Bank in 1898 (Page 20)
- W. H. Streeter was president of the First National Bank from its founding until his death in 1907 (Page 20)
- T. E. Williams became president in 1907 and served until his retirement in 1917 (Page 20)

- In 1920, the average farm size was 179.7 acres (Page 14)
- In 1997, there were 697 farms averaging 507 acres (Page 14)
- By 2002, there were 603 farms averaging 577 acres (Page 14)
- In 2002, Hamilton County ranked first in Nebraska in the value of crops produced (Page 14)
- Hamilton County annually receives approximately twenty-six inches of precipitation (Page 14)
- Irrigation canals and wells first appeared in Hamilton County in the late 1930s (Page 15)
- In August 1940, The Aurora News published a photo comparing a successful irrigated corn crop (80 bushels) to a failed dryland crop (Page 15)
- By February 1955, the 500th well was drilled, and the county was declared "The Deepwell Irrigation Center of the Nation" (Page 15)
- By the late 1960s, there were approximately 1,600 registered wells irrigating over 100,000 acres (Page 15)
- In the early 1970s, center-pivot irrigation systems reached the county, leading to a rapid conversion of rangeland to cropland (Page 15)
- By the late 1970s, about 89% of the county's area was cropland, with 81% irrigated and 19% dryfarmed (Page 15)
- In the early 1980s, the number of irrigation wells had increased to over 2,600 (Page 15)
- As of the time of writing, Hamilton County has 3,361 irrigation wells that water just over 400,000 acres (Page 15)
- The first farmers' elevator in Hordville incorporated in 1906, and by 1915 all communities had elevators (Page 15)
- In 1921, Burr and Buck claimed Hamilton is the only county in Nebraska, or probably any other state, with a farmers' elevator at every railroad station (Page 16)
- Grain elevators in Hamilton County's communities are the largest structures and serve as one of each town's focal points (Page 16)
- Many of the county's original towns are no longer present due to population shifts related to changing economic issues and transportation patterns (Page 16)
- Baltensperger contends that town development became heavily dependent on rail connections (Page 16)
- The town of Hamilton, founded by J. F. and T. H. Glover, was an active place in 1874-75 but lost its businesses and houses when the county seat was located in Aurora (Page 16)
- Most early settlements like Alvin, Avon, Buckeye, Bunker Hill, Cedar Valley, Leonard, Lerton, Mirimichi, Orville City, Otis, Penn, Shiloh, Stockham, St. Joe, and Williamsport have disappeared (Page 17)
- Of the remaining towns, Giltner, Hampton, Marquette, Murphy, and Phillips are located on the railroad (Page 17)
- Towns were platted as square blocks and designed as T-Towns, with Main Street beginning at the railroad tracks (Page 17)
- Five of the seven rural communities peaked in population between 1900 and 1940 (Page 17)
- Four of those five communities have demonstrated recent population gains (Page 17)
- Aurora peaked in population at the most recent census in 2000 with 4,225 citizens and has steadily increased since 1940 (Page 17)
- Farm consolidation is expected to make it difficult for towns outside of Aurora to maintain their populations (Page 17)
- Pat Dinslage (1992) discusses population declines in Hordville (pop. 150) and Polk (pop. 322), noting their dependence on farming communities (Page 18)
- Bradley Baltensperger (1985) describes county seat disputes in frontier Nebraska as involving fraudulent elections, theft of records, and court battles (Page 18)
- Orville City was selected as the first county seat in 1871 but was challenged for being too far southeast (Page 18)
- In the first election, Aurora received over two-thirds of the votes but the results were deemed illegal (Page 18)
- A second vote in 1874 required 399.5 votes; Aurora collected 399, failing by half a vote (Page 18)
- Aurora citizens took possession of the county courthouse and records by force in 1874 (Page 18)
- Darius Wilcox lobbied the state legislature to change the requirement to three-fifths of votes cast (Page 18)
- A special election in May saw Aurora win by a small majority, while Hamilton won the June election by a slim margin (Page 18)
- The fifth and final vote in October 1875 resulted in Aurora receiving 481 votes and Hamilton 400, making Aurora the official seat of government in early 1876 (Page 18)
- After the election, Hamilton and Orville merged with Aurora, and Hamilton became a "deserted village" (Page 18)
- In 1871, David Stone represented a group of men from Lucas County, Iowa, who wished to establish a town in Hamilton County (Page 18)
- The town of Aurora was founded in 1871 at a point on Lincoln Creek where two cottonwood trees stood (Page 19)
- The site is now part of Streeter Park (HM01-243) (Page 19)
- David Stone erected the "first frame building in the town" in August 1871, a store and residence (Page 19)
- The town was named for Stone's hometown, Aurora, Illinois (Page 19)
- Aurora was incorporated on July 3, 1877 (Page 19)
- The Burlington and Missouri Railroad arrived in 1879, which was a major turning point (Page 19)
- The railroad required a $72,000 bond, with $48,000 due when the line reached Aurora (Page 19)
- A vote on the bond resulted in 956 votes in favor and 238 opposed out of 1,194 cast (Page 19)
- The bond amount was lowered to $50,000 due to public support (Page 19)
- The first regular train ran into Aurora on October 14, 1879 (Page 19)
- The railroad extended lines from Aurora west to Grand Island (1884) and north to Central City (1886) (Page 19)
- Aurora was Hamilton County's primary city in the late 1800s and early 1900s (Page 20)
- Early enterprises included a cigar factory, a broom factory, and a washing machine company (Page 20)
- The Temple Craft Association was formed in 1888 by thirty-one men to promote Aurora's business community (Page 20)
- Fourteen leading business men pledged $25,000 in capital for the Temple Craft project (Page 20)
- The Hamilton County Bank was established in 1877 by George Wildish (Page 20)
- The Farmers' and Merchants' Bank was established in 1883 by Streeter, Hainer, and Farley (Page 20)
- Several banks merged to form the First National Bank in 1898 (Page 20)
- W. H. Streeter was president of the First National Bank from its founding until his death in 1907 (Page 20)
- T. E. Williams became president in 1907 and served until his retirement in 1917 (Page 20)

In the late 1800s and early 1900s, Aurora blossomed as Hamilton County's primary city, dominating both business and government affairs. Bradford (1979) states that the "business life of Aurora in the late nineteenth century was extremely vital and, of course, influenced the extent and the demand of the cultural life."[68] Early enterprises included a cigar factory, a broom factory, and a washing machine company.[69] These were not individual efforts; leading citizens often joined forces to help Aurora prosper. Fuse (2004) in the Aurora News-Register points out that Aurora has a long history of community spirit and economic development. An excellent example is the Temple Craft Association formed in 1888 by thirty-one men to promote Aurora's business community; the Temple Craft building remains and is located on the southwest corner of  $12^{\text{th}}$  and M Streets in Aurora (HM01-186).<sup>70</sup> Fourteen of Aurora's leading business men pledged $25,000 in capital for the project and the associations' bylaws stated that the "object of the project was to encourage building, improvement and to promote the material prosperity of Aurora."<sup>71</sup> This association was just one catalyst impacting Aurora's business community which ultimately spurred others to invest in the community. In addition to the associations and factories, banks and mercantile establishments dominated Aurora's business community. The Hamilton County Bank was established in 1877 by George Wildish; Wildish was later bought out by W. H. Streeter in 1886. $^{72}$  In 1883, Streeter along with E. J. Hainer and W. I. Farley had established the Farmers' and Merchants' Bank; Streeter later withdrew in 1886 to head the Hamilton County Bank. T. E. Williams arrived in Aurora in 1888 from Eau Claire, Wisconsin to accept the position of cashier in the Farmers' and Merchants' Bank. $^{73}$  Several banks (Aurora Banking Company, Hamilton County Bank, Farmer's and Merchants' Bank) merged over the next decade and First National Bank appeared in 1898. W. H. Streeter was the president and remained in that capacity until his death in 1907, at which time T. E. Williams was elected president, a position he held until his retirement in 1917. $^{74}$

In the late 1800s and early 1900s, Aurora blossomed as Hamilton County's primary city, dominating both business and government affairs. Bradford (1979) states that the "business life of Aurora in the late nineteenth century was extremely vital and, of course, influenced the extent and the demand of the cultural life."[68] Early enterprises included a cigar factory, a broom factory, and a washing machine company.[69] These were not individual efforts; leading citizens often joined forces to help Aurora prosper. Fuse (2004) in the Aurora News-Register points out that Aurora has a long history of community spirit and economic development. An excellent example is the Temple Craft Association formed in 1888 by thirty-one men to promote Aurora's business community; the Temple Craft building remains and is located on the southwest corner of  $12^{\text{th}}$  and M Streets in Aurora (HM01-186).<sup>70</sup> Fourteen of Aurora's leading business men pledged $25,000 in capital for the project and the associations' bylaws stated that the "object of the project was to encourage building, improvement and to promote the material prosperity of Aurora."<sup>71</sup> This association was just one catalyst impacting Aurora's business community which ultimately spurred others to invest in the community. In addition to the associations and factories, banks and mercantile establishments dominated Aurora's business community. The Hamilton County Bank was established in 1877 by George Wildish; Wildish was later bought out by W. H. Streeter in 1886. $^{72}$  In 1883, Streeter along with E. J. Hainer and W. I. Farley had established the Farmers' and Merchants' Bank; Streeter later withdrew in 1886 to head the Hamilton County Bank. T. E. Williams arrived in Aurora in 1888 from Eau Claire, Wisconsin to accept the position of cashier in the Farmers' and Merchants' Bank. $^{73}$  Several banks (Aurora Banking Company, Hamilton County Bank, Farmer's and Merchants' Bank) merged over the next decade and First National Bank appeared in 1898. W. H. Streeter was the president and remained in that capacity until his death in 1907, at which time T. E. Williams was elected president, a position he held until his retirement in 1917. $^{74}$
